section_summary: This section documents Japanese propaganda, cultural diplomacy, commercial outreach, military contacts, and suspected intelligence activity in Chile from 1932 through 1940. It includes embassy and consular reports on pro-Japanese literature, press coverage, an Osaka YMCA Spanish-language supplement, trade and cultural exchanges, and Japanese interest in Chilean arms purchases and coastal land. Later records concern Japanese travelers arrested for photographing northern Chile from an aircraft, while several cross-references and an enclosed consular report also discuss German and Nazi activity in southern Chile.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1337: Distribution by Japanese Legation of Literature on the Manchurian Situation
subfiles.from: R. Henry Norweb, U.S. chargé d’affaires ad interim, Santiago
subfiles.about: Reports the Japanese Legation’s distribution of pro-Japanese pamphlets and use of radio commentary in Chile.
subfiles.summary: Norweb reports that the Japanese minister widely distributed three English- or Spanish-language publications defending Japan’s position in Manchuria and China. Recipients reportedly included the Chilean Foreign Office, diplomatic corps, newspapers, universities, and schools. A University of Concepción professor also delivered a radio talk favorable to Japan.

subfiles.title: Confirmation Copy of Despatch No. 1337
subfiles.from: R. Henry Norweb, U.S. chargé d’affaires ad interim, Santiago
subfiles.about: Duplicates the report on Japanese distribution of literature concerning Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: This confirmation copy repeats the report that the Japanese minister circulated three publications defending Japanese policy in Manchuria and China. It lists their authors and describes distribution to official, diplomatic, press, and educational audiences. It also notes a pro-Japanese radio address by a University of Concepción professor.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Report No. 1986: Propaganda Film on Manchukuo
subfiles.from: U.S. military attaché in Chile
subfiles.about: Refers to a military attaché report on the showing of a propaganda film about Manchukuo.
subfiles.summary: The sheet directs readers to a motion-picture file containing Report No. 1986. That report covered an August 1–5 showing of a film on Manchukuo and its government, arranged at the Japanese minister’s request.

subfiles.title: Report No. 2403: Visit to Chile of Colonel Chikaide Okuda
subfiles.from: U.S. military attaché, Santiago
subfiles.to: Office of the Chief of Staff
subfiles.about: Reports a Japanese Army colonel’s South American tour to collect information on military livestock.
subfiles.summary: Colonel Chikaide Okuda of the Imperial Japanese Army spent several days in Santiago after visiting Argentina and possibly other South American countries. Newspapers and personal contacts indicated that he was gathering information on horses and mules used by mounted army units.

subfiles.title: Japanese Propaganda in Chile
subfiles.from: Renwick S. McNiece, American consul, Valparaíso
subfiles.about: Transmits two English-language Japanese propaganda pamphlets distributed through a merchant in Valparaíso.
subfiles.summary: McNiece encloses “The Significance of the China Affair” and the Japanese prime minister’s address “Preparing Ourselves for the Emergency.” The Japanese government’s commercial agent in Santiago had given the pamphlets to a Valparaíso merchant for distribution.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 16: Chilean Relations with Japan
subfiles.from: Norman Armour, U.S. ambassador, Santiago
subfiles.about: Describes Chilean press publicity and changing trade figures associated with the Japanese emperor’s birthday.
subfiles.summary: Armour reports extensive favorable press coverage of Japan, Japanese-Chilean trade, and Japanese economic progress on the emperor’s birthday. El Diario Ilustrado defended Japan’s actions in China as an anti-communist service, while Japanese commercial interests purchased prominent advertising. Chilean imports from Japan had nearly tripled in the first quarter of 1938, although Chilean exports to Japan declined.

subfiles.title: Duplicate Copy of Despatch No. 16: Chilean Relations with Japan
subfiles.from: Norman Armour, U.S. ambassador, Santiago
subfiles.about: Duplicates the report on favorable Japanese publicity and Chilean-Japanese trade.
subfiles.summary: This copy repeats the embassy’s account of favorable Chilean press treatment of Japan on the emperor’s birthday. It notes El Diario Ilustrado’s anti-communist defense of Japanese policy in China and the sharp rise in Chilean purchases from Japan. The increase is linked to Japanese trade promotion and Chile’s search for markets.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 169: Japanese Propaganda in Chile
subfiles.from: Norman Armour, U.S. ambassador, Santiago
subfiles.about: Transmits Spanish-language Japanese pamphlets and reports favorable comments by returning Chilean law students.
subfiles.summary: Armour forwards two Spanish pamphlets presenting Japan’s viewpoint toward China. He also notes the return of Chilean law students invited to Japan by the Japanese government. Delegation leader Federico Duncker Biggs publicly praised the group’s reception in Japan, California, and Germany.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on Osaka YMCA Propaganda
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.about: Advises against approaching the American YMCA about propaganda issued by the Osaka YMCA.
subfiles.summary: The Far Eastern Affairs Division concludes that no useful purpose would be served by contacting the American YMCA administration. It explains that the Japanese YMCA was independent despite American funding for advisory secretaries. The memorandum recalls the Tokyo YMCA auditorium’s use for anti-American meetings after passage of the 1924 Immigration Act.

subfiles.title: American Republics Note Suggesting Consultation with the YMCA
subfiles.from: Division of the American Republics, Department of State
subfiles.about: Suggests informally raising objectionable Japanese propaganda with the YMCA administration.
subfiles.summary: The note asks whether the Far Eastern Division might wish to approach the YMCA administration informally. Its concern is the objectionable character of Japanese propaganda distributed under the YMCA name.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 530: Transmitting Pro-Japanese Propaganda Sponsored by the Osaka YMCA
subfiles.from: Norman Armour, U.S. ambassador, Santiago
subfiles.about: Forwards a Spanish-language Osaka YMCA supplement containing Japanese propaganda.
subfiles.summary: The embassy transmits two copies of a February 1939 Spanish supplement published by the Osaka YMCA. A prominent member of the American community had objected to the use of the YMCA name for such propaganda, and the embassy agreed that the association was inappropriate.

subfiles.title: Los Jóvenes en Osaka: Spanish Supplement
subfiles.from: Osaka YMCA
subfiles.to: Spanish-speaking readers, especially in Latin America
subfiles.about: Presents Japanese wartime, cultural, diplomatic, and economic propaganda for Spanish-speaking audiences.
subfiles.summary: The supplement portrays Japan as the guardian of Asian civilization and its war in China as a struggle against communism and disorder. It promotes Japanese-Peruvian cultural and commercial cooperation, celebrates German-Japanese relations and the Anti-Comintern Pact, and describes the Berlin–Tokyo Condor flight. Other articles praise the sacrifice of soldier Yutaka Asakura and discuss Manchukuo’s development budget and five-year plan.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 288: Pro-Japanese Editorial in El Mercurio
subfiles.from: Claude G. Bowers, U.S. ambassador, Santiago
subfiles.about: Transmits an editorial defending Japan’s war in China and reports Ambassador Kawai’s visit to Chile.
subfiles.summary: Bowers forwards the original and a translation of an El Mercurio editorial portraying Japanese action in China as necessary to suppress Bolshevism. The editorial hoped negotiations with Wang Ching-wei would create a new Chinese regime. Its publication coincided with Japanese Ambassador Kawai’s visit to Santiago to inspect diplomatic posts and explore expanded commerce.

subfiles.title: El Mercurio Editorial: “Perspectivas en Oriente”
subfiles.from: El Mercurio
subfiles.about: Argues that Japanese expansion is restoring order in China and opening commercial prospects for South America.
subfiles.summary: The editorial depicts Japan as protecting Asian civilization against Soviet-inspired communism and denies that its expansion is conquest. It favors a Japan-China-Manchukuo political and economic alignment and the creation of a new regime under Wang Ching-wei. Chile and other South American countries are urged to recognize the resulting commercial opportunities.

subfiles.title: Translation of “Perspectivas en Oriente”
subfiles.from: American Embassy, Santiago
subfiles.about: Provides an English translation of El Mercurio’s pro-Japanese editorial.
subfiles.summary: The translation presents Japan as a constructive force opposing Soviet penetration and political disorder in China. It argues that Western and South American countries will benefit from restored order and commerce. It also expresses hope that Wang Ching-wei’s negotiations with Japan will soon establish a new central Chinese regime.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: Japanese Activities in Chile and Departure of Yoshitaro Amano
subfiles.from: Claude G. Bowers, U.S. ambassador, Chile
subfiles.about: Refers to a report on Yoshitaro Amano’s departure for Panama and the management of his farm.
subfiles.summary: The sheet points to Despatch No. 560 and Vice Consul McLain’s report from Concepción. It notes that Yoshitaro Amano, owner of Andalién Farm, departed for Panama and identifies Asai as the farm manager.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 560: The German Problem in Southern Chile
subfiles.from: Claude G. Bowers, U.S. ambassador, Santiago
subfiles.to: Secretary and Under Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Forwards consular observations about Nazi influence, a German travel agency, and suspicious activity on Esmeralda Island.
subfiles.summary: Bowers discusses the large, strongly Nazi German population between Concepción and Puerto Montt and the possibility of a German minority problem or coup. He highlights reports concerning the German-owned Impresa Andina del Sur and suspicious activity on Esmeralda Island, where two approaching men were reportedly killed. Bowers informed the Chilean foreign minister confidentially of the reports.

subfiles.title: McLain Letter on Japanese and German Activities in South-Central Chile
subfiles.from: Camden L. McLain, American vice consul, Concepción
subfiles.to: Claude G. Bowers, U.S. ambassador, Santiago
subfiles.about: Reports no detected Japanese activity around Concepción but provides information on Japanese residents and alleged Nazi organization in southern Chile.
subfiles.summary: McLain found no suspicious Japanese activity around Concepción after consulting bankers, customs brokers, and merchants. He reports Yoshitaro Amano’s departure and identifies S. Asai as manager of Andalién Farm. Most of the letter concerns German dominance and Nazi sentiment in southern Chile, including allegations about a travel agency, Esmeralda Island, a pro-German radio station, and a former meat-packing plant used as a training center.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: Japanese Coastal Colonization and Commercial Agreement
subfiles.from: Claude G. Bowers, U.S. ambassador, Chile
subfiles.about: Refers to a report that Japan sought large coastal tracts in Chile and was negotiating a compensatory commercial agreement.
subfiles.summary: The sheet points to Despatch No. 552 in another file. That report concerned alleged Japanese efforts to acquire extensive land along Chile’s coast for colonization and advanced negotiations for a Chilean-Japanese compensation trade agreement.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: Chilean Purchase of Arms and Munitions from Japan
subfiles.from: U.S. Navy Department
subfiles.about: Refers to negotiations for Chilean purchases of Japanese arms and munitions.
subfiles.summary: The referenced letter reported negotiations between the Chilean minister of war and the Showa Trading Company. It also stated that the Japanese minister in Chile was actively promoting the transaction.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: Reports on Japanese Activities from Concepción and Valparaíso
subfiles.from: Claude G. Bowers, U.S. ambassador, Chile
subfiles.about: Refers to consular reports concerning Japanese activities in Concepción and Valparaíso.
subfiles.summary: The sheet directs readers to Despatch No. 541 in a related file. The underlying despatch compiled reports from the U.S. consulates at Concepción and Valparaíso about Japanese activities in Chile.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 174: Arrest of Japanese Photographers
subfiles.from: Claude G. Bowers, U.S. ambassador, Santiago
subfiles.to: Secretary of State, Washington; confidential for the Under Secretary
subfiles.about: Reports the arrest of two Japanese travelers and a Chilean suspected of espionage after aerial photography.
subfiles.summary: Souji Indo and Goro Miyazaki were arrested for taking photographs while flying from Vallenar to Santiago on a National Air Line aircraft. Their companion, Manuel Sigren, was a former Chilean consul in Baltimore suspected of foreign espionage. Officials were also interested in an unexplained check for 800,000 pesos received by Sigren.

subfiles.title: Department of State Receipt and Routing Sheet for Telegram No. 174
subfiles.from: Department of State
subfiles.about: Records departmental receipt and routing of the telegram concerning the Japanese arrests.
subfiles.summary: The sheet contains receipt, filing, and routing stamps dated July 24–25, 1940. It directed the associated telegram through the Department of State’s A-B office and to officials including Welles and Warren.

subfiles.title: Under Secretary’s Instruction to Notify the FBI
subfiles.from: Sumner Welles, under secretary of state
subfiles.about: Orders immediate transmission of the arrest information to the FBI if it had not already been sent.
subfiles.summary: Referring to Santiago Telegram No. 174, the under secretary instructs Fletcher Warren to send the information to the Federal Bureau of Investigation at once. The instruction shows that the suspected espionage incident was treated as relevant to U.S. domestic security authorities.

subfiles.title: Letter to J. Edgar Hoover Concerning the Japanese Arrests
subfiles.from: Fletcher Warren, executive assistant to Assistant Secretary Berle
subfiles.to: J. Edgar Hoover, director, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.about: Confirms telephone notification to the FBI and supplies a paraphrase of the Santiago telegram.
subfiles.summary: Warren confirms an earlier telephone conversation with the FBI and quotes a paraphrase of Ambassador Bowers’s telegram. The letter identifies Goro Miyazaki, Souji Indo, and Manuel Sigren and describes the aerial photography, Sigren’s former Baltimore post, espionage suspicions, and unexplained 800,000-peso check.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: Japanese Efforts to Improve Prestige in Chile
subfiles.from: Claude G. Bowers, U.S. ambassador, Chile
subfiles.about: Refers to a report on hostile Chilean opinion and Japanese cultural diplomacy.
subfiles.summary: The referenced despatch stated that Chilean public opinion remained unfriendly toward Japan despite the Japanese minister’s efforts. Circumstances reportedly forced him to associate mainly with German and Italian representatives. Formation of a Japanese-Chilean Cultural Society was described as the sole concrete achievement in improving Japan’s prestige.

subfiles.title: Attaché’s Report: Arrest of Japanese Photographers and Manuel Sigren
subfiles.from: U.S. attaché in Chile
subfiles.to: Office of Naval Intelligence, U.S. Navy Department
subfiles.about: Provides additional details about the arrest of two Japanese men and their Chilean companion on suspicion of espionage.
subfiles.summary: The report states that Souji Indo and Goro Miyazaki accompanied Manuel Sigren to his cobalt mine in northern Chile. A National Air Lines pilot saw the Japanese passengers taking photographs on the return flight, and all three men were arrested upon landing in Santiago. Sigren was described as an unscrupulous businessman, former Chilean consul in Baltimore, former Turkish Legation secretary, and suspected spy with an unexplained 800,000-peso check.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: Japanese Cultural Offensive in Chile
subfiles.from: Claude G. Bowers, U.S. ambassador, Chile
subfiles.about: Refers to a later report on the Japanese cultural offensive in Chile.
subfiles.summary: The sheet points to Despatch No. 993 in the file on the Chilean-Japanese Cultural Institute. The underlying document reported activities associated with Japan’s cultural campaign in Chile.
